sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies Jesus as the true vine fulfilling Israel's vine imagery, with the Father as vinedresser who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones, and the disciples as already clean through the word Jesus has spoken.
sections.relevance: The passage describes branches 'in me' (en emoi) that do not bear fruit and are removed by the vinedresser. The neutral reading emphasizes that the fruitless branches are not outsiders but are described as connected to Jesus, consistent with the Judas pattern -- one chosen by Jesus who was 'not clean.' The vinedresser responds to the branch's condition (fruitful or fruitless); the branch's status determines the Father's action (removal or pruning). This implies that being connected to Jesus does not automatically determine the outcome -- the branch's condition matters.
key_phrases: Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away
every branch that bears fruit, he prunes it
You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you

sections.section_title: The Imperative to Abide and Its Consequences
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the command to abide as an imperative assuming the genuine possibility of not abiding, with the consequence of not abiding being removal, withering, and burning, and the consequence of abiding being fruitfulness, answered prayer, and the Father's glorification.
sections.relevance: The imperative 'abide in me' (meinate en emoi) is a command addressed to the disciples as agents who must act. The neutral reading states: 'The disciples are not told that they automatically abide or that their abiding is assured; they are told to abide. The command assumes the possibility of not abiding -- otherwise the imperative would be meaningless.' The conditional 'if anyone does not abide in me' (ean me tis mene en emoi) is identified as a third-class conditional indicating a real possibility. The consequence -- thrown out, dried up, gathered, burned -- is described as a complete process of removal and destruction with no indication of reattachment. The neutral reading explicitly contrasts 6:37 ('the one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out') with 15:6: 'The difference is between the coming and the abiding -- between initial approach and sustained connection.' This directly presents human beings as genuine agents whose ongoing choice to abide determines their outcome, and it is the core of the author's argument in this passage, not an aside or illustration.
key_phrases: Abide in me, and I in you
the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine
apart from me you can do nothing
If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away as a branch and dries up; and they gather them, and throw them into the fire, and they are burned
If you abide in me and my words abide in you

sections.section_title: The Chain of Love and Abiding in Love
sections.summary: The neutral reading traces a chain of love from Father to Son to disciples, with abiding in Jesus's love conditioned on keeping his commandments, paralleling Jesus's own obedience to the Father's commandments as the basis for abiding in the Father's love.
sections.relevance: The conditional 'if you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love' presents human obedience as the mechanism that sustains the relationship. The neutral reading states explicitly: 'The abiding is not unconditional; it depends on keeping the commandments.' The parallel with Jesus's own obedience to the Father reinforces the pattern: the relationship is maintained through active responsiveness, not through a static guarantee. This implies genuine human agency in maintaining standing before God, though the section addresses the mechanism of abiding rather than directly stating salvation outcomes.
key_phrases: If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love
just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the love commandment as the singular distillation of all commandments, defines friendship with Jesus as conditional on ongoing obedience, and identifies Jesus's choosing of the disciples as the initiative that established the relationship -- an initiative that includes Judas, who was chosen but departed.
sections.relevance: John 15:16 ('You did not choose me but I chose you') is conventionally cited by the deterministic/Calvinist side to prove that God unilaterally determines who will be saved -- that election is unconditional and irrevocable. The neutral reading reveals that the choosing is about Jesus's initiative in calling the disciples to a mission ('appointed you that you would go and bear fruit'), not about the deterministic guarantee of individual salvation. The neutral reading states: 'The choosing and the appointing do not eliminate the conditions of abiding stated in the preceding verses. Jesus chose the twelve, including Judas (6:70), and Judas proved to be a fruitless branch. The choosing establishes the relationship; the abiding sustains it. Election initiates; obedience and love maintain.' The section also presents friendship as conditional ('You are my friends if you do what I command you,' v. 14), reinforcing that the election-to-relationship requires ongoing human response. The conventional use treats the choosing as the whole story; the neutral reading shows it is the beginning of a story that includes conditions the chosen must meet.
key_phrases: You did not choose me but I chose you, and appointed you that you would go and bear fruit
You are my friends if you do what I command you
This is my commandment, that you love one another

sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies this section as explaining why the world hates the disciples: because Jesus chose them out of the world-system, they no longer belong to it, and the world responds to their defection with hostility, just as it responded to Jesus with hostility.

sections.section_title: The Words, the Works, and the Hatred Without Cause
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus's words and works as evidence that removes all pretext for unbelief, making the rejection of Jesus a culpable human act -- a genuine seeing followed by a genuine choosing of hatred over belief.
sections.relevance: The language of excuse and culpability assumes genuine human agency. The neutral reading states: 'Before the light came, there was ignorance; after the light comes, there is willful rejection.' The phrase 'they have no excuse for their sin' (prophasin ouk echousin) and 'they have both seen and hated' presuppose that the rejecters had genuine capacity to respond otherwise. If God had unilaterally determined their rejection, the language of excuse, pretext, and culpable seeing-then-hating would be incoherent. The text assumes the words and works constituted a genuine opportunity that was genuinely refused.
key_phrases: now they have no excuse for their sin
they have both seen and hated me and my Father as well
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin
They hated me without a cause

sections.section_title: The Spirit's Testimony and the Disciples' Witness
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies the Spirit as the parakletos (advocate) who will testify about Jesus alongside the disciples' own eyewitness testimony, equipping the community for witness in the face of the world's hostility.
